Here are some practical things to look for when shopping for a new electric guitar, based on what you’ve already been discussing (Strat vs Les Paul, Les Paul tone/uses, open D setup and coil-tap ideas):

- Body & construction: try both body types (e.g., Strat-style contoured bolt-on vs Les Paul single-cut, set-neck) and notice how each feels in your hands and on your body—comfort and balance matter for long playing sessions.

- Neck profile & playability: check the neck shape and fretboard feel. A neck that’s comfortable for your fretting hand will make a big difference, especially if you plan to do fingerpicking or fast lead work.

- Pickups & tonal options: listen for the pickups’ character—Les Pauls are described as warm, rich, and sustaining (great for rock/ heavier styles); Strat-style guitars tend to have brighter, spankier tones. If you want more versatility, look for coil-tap/coil-splitting options to get single-coil-like tones from humbuckers.

- Setup & stringing: play the guitar with strings similar to what you’ll use. If you plan to use alternate tunings like open D, the assistant advice noted heavier gauges can help (heavier strings give fuller tone and handle lower tunings better). Also check the action and intonation—low action that doesn’t buzz and good intonation are important.

- Acoustic-like fingerpicking: if you want to play acoustic-style fingerpicked parts (you asked about Les Paul and "Blackbird" style), test how a solid-body electric responds to finger attack—neck pickup position and string choice influence clarity; try both guitars to see which feels and sounds better for that approach.

- Electronics & hardware condition: test pots, switches, tremolo (if present), and tuners for smooth operation and no crackling. If considering used instruments, check for any repairs or damage.

- Amplifier/rig: always try the guitar through an amp you like (bring your own if possible) so you hear its tone in a realistic context.

- Play what you love: bring a few songs or licks you know well (including any alternate-tuning pieces if relevant) and play them on each guitar to compare feel and tone.

If you tell me whether you’re leaning toward a Strat or Les Paul (or want something versatile with coil-splitting), I can give more specific checklist items to test in the store.
